studies.engineAndLocalSteps: The public engine has no iterative targeting or projectile simulator. The local model launches a fixed-speed candidate at a guessed angle, integrates gravity and linear drag with velocity before position, interpolates ground contact, measures signed range error, and refines a sign-changing angle bracket by bisection. Exported engine sine and cosine provide deterministic launch components; no engine behaviour is claimed.
studies.example: A harbour launcher searches for an angle that lands at a stationary drum on level ground.
specClaims: A 30-degree launch resolves into horizontal speed 5 times square root of 3 and vertical speed 5; its first drag/gravity step has vertical speed 3.9 and height 0.39.
Ground contact is interpolated between the last positive-height point and the first non-positive point.
The default midpoint guesses begin at 20 and 30 degrees, halve their angle bracket and accept only a completed impact within tolerance.
Reducing only the midpoint budget to 2 retains the same initial candidates and fails outside tolerance.
An already acceptable endpoint uses no midpoint guesses; a same-side bracket is rejected without claiming every intermediate angle is impossible.
An unfinished flight supplies no invented impact, and changed drag can make an accepted prediction miss under different physics.
Drawing bounds, chart samples, moments, live input endpoints and prose placeholders remain consistent.
limitations: The search targets the local discrete simulator, not continuous physical truth or the scene engine.
Only a stationary, equal-height ground target and one angle bracket are handled; no obstacle or moving-target search is supplied.
Bracketing assumes a continuous error function and does not select among multiple arcs.
Unfinished-flight runs omit the error chart and comparison because their impact error is unknown.
The opening frame is an endpoint diagnostic, with midpoint guesses on later frames; terminal endpoint decisions are held for one playback interval.
No verified targeting-specific public implementation was added; the GSL manual is cited only for the numerical method.

studies.engineAndLocalSteps: The straight run-up calls the exported engine matchVelocity for acceleration. Local code advances horizontal motion, recognises the first sampled marker encounter, checks both position and velocity tolerances, applies a vertical launch impulse only on acceptance, and evaluates a constant-gravity equal-height flight from the actual accepted horizontal state. No engine jump or private helper is imported.
studies.example: Courier Finch runs to a take-off ring to cross a canal onto a receiving pad.
specClaims: The first run-up requests acceleration 16, caps it at 4, and advances to speed 1 and position 0.25.
The default run reaches the marker at time 2.25, position 7.5 and horizontal speed 4, then applies vertical speed 5.
The exact equal-height flight lasts 2 seconds, reaches apex height 2.5 at x 11.5 and contacts the pad at x 15.5.
Changing only the initial position to 6 reaches the correct marker at time 0.75 with speed 3, so launch is rejected with velocity error 1.
Position alone and velocity alone cannot pass; actual tolerance-accepted horizontal speed is preserved.
A skipped position window, an unreachable speed and an accepted state that misses a narrow receiving pad are genuine failure cases.
An unfinished bounded run reports its remaining phase; drawing bounds, charts, moments, inputs and placeholders remain consistent.
limitations: The local marker policy is a one-pass decision on a straight, aligned runway; it is not a general spatial arrival controller.
Sampled encounters can skip the launch window. Rejected runs end at the decision, retaining the incoming velocity without simulating emergency braking.
Flight assumes equal heights, constant gravity, no drag and no mid-air steering.
Tolerance-accepted launch errors can still miss a narrow receiving pad.
The final landing sample retains incoming velocity and ends before collision response.
The scene engine supplies run-up acceleration only; it has no jump-marker transition.
